items.title: Agents are sessions, not requests: size GKE node pools for AI agent sessions
items.summary: AI agent sessions remain active and idle for most of the workday, making traditional one-Pod-per-session allocations inefficient for cluster resources. By using open-source tools like Agent Substrate and AX on GKE, developers can park idle sessions in object storage to release compute resources while maintaining session state. This approach optimizes resource utilization and reduces Kubernetes node costs by up to 40%.

items.title: Distributed LLM Training Across Metros: Streaming DiLoCo in MaxText
items.summary: Streaming DiLoCo in MaxText enables developers to efficiently train large language models across geographically distributed TPU slices by streaming parameter fragments instead of synchronizing full models at every step. This approach slashes cross-slice communication volume by over 60× and eliminates network stalls, allowing seamless multi-datacenter scaling without degrading model convergence or quality.

items.title: Did the user ask for this? Securing AI agents against intent hijacking with Semantic governance policies
items.summary: Semantic governance policies protect AI agents from indirect prompt injection and intent hijacking by validating every proposed tool call against user intent and natural language constraints before execution. items.title: Announcing Long-Context Training on TPUs with MaxText Context Parallelism

items.title: 6 Years of React: Architecture Lessons That Actually Scale
items.summary: I'm Mohd Zakir Hassan, a Tech Lead with 6+ years of building React applications used by thousands of people. These are the habits that have held up as teams and products grew. If a component fetches data, formats it, and renders a complex UI, split it. Containers handle data; presentational components handle looks. Keep server state (data from APIs) separate from UI state (is this modal open?). Tools like React Query for server state and plain React state for UI cover most needs before you reach for a global store. /features/billing/ beats /components, /hooks, /utils once the app gets big. Use the React Profiler and real user metrics. Most slowness comes from a few heavy re-renders or oversized bundles, not from everywhere. Short-lived JWTs, refresh tokens in httpOnly cookies, and role checks on the server, never only in the UI. As a Tech Lead, the biggest lever I have is code review: small, frequent, and focused on structure over style. Originally published at zakirhassan.github.io. I write about React, scalable systems and AI from Kanpur, India.

items.title: Where a lunar-calendar app actually breaks: time zones, true solar time, and caching
items.summary: Every time someone asks me how to build an "AI astrology" app, they assume the hard part is the model. It isn't. The hard part is that the calendar underneath is a moving target, and every bug shows up as a vague complaint: "the chart is wrong." I build Taoly, a Chinese Four Pillars (Bazi) tool. Here are the four places it actually broke, in the order they cost me the most time. In Bazi, the month pillar is decided by solar terms, not by the Gregorian month. So "born in March" tells you nothing until you know whether the birth fell before or after 惊蛰. Chinese hour pillars split the day into 12 two-hour blocks (时辰), and the boundary behaviour around 23:00 differs between schools. items.title: I built a browser test that proves when a mouse sensor loses tracking (and got my refund with it)
items.summary: Short story long, I bought a budget gaming mouse and something felt off in Valorant: slow aiming was fine, but hard flicks moved the crosshair far less than my hand did, and sometimes it snapped backwards. The usual online mouse testers check buttons, double-clicks and polling rate. None of them could show the seller what was actually happening. So I built one that can. If the mouse moves the exact same physical distance every time, a healthy sensor reports the same number of counts, no matter how fast you move. So: Put two hard stops on the mousepad (books, a ruler, the pad's edges). Do a few slow swipes between them. Their median becomes the baseline. Flick hard between the same stops. Any fast swipe more than 10% off the baseline is flagged: SHORT (lost movement), LONG (added movement) or spin-out (movement reported backwards). requestPointerLock({ unadjustedMovement: true }) gives raw HID deltas in Chrome and Edge, so OS acceleration and pointer speed can't skew anything. pointerrawupdate delivers every report the mouse sends (up to 1000 Hz and beyond). items.title: Why Optimistic UI Updates Make Your Apps Feel Instant
items.summary: What Are Optimistic UI Updates? An optimistic UI update is a frontend design pattern where a web application immediately updates its screen to show the result of a user's action before getting confirmation from the backend server. Instead of freezing the screen or displaying a loading spinner while waiting for a network request—the process of sending data across the internet to a remote server—the app acts optimistic. It predicts that the server request will succeed 99% of the time, updates the interface instantly, and syncs with the database in the background. If the request unexpectedly fails, the app catches the error and silently rolls the user interface back to its original state. Imagine sending a text message on your smartphone. When you tap "Send," your message immediately pops up in a green or blue chat bubble inside the conversation window. You don't sit staring at a blank screen for three seconds while your phone contacts a cell tower, routes data through telecom servers, and confirms delivery. items.title: A checklist for the remove.bg API shutdown on December 1
items.summary: remove.bg’s self-serve API shuts down on December 1, 2026, at 9:00 a.m. CET. If your app still calls it, here’s what to check before then. remove.bg FAQ Find every integration. Search your code for api.remove.bg. Check dependencies too, especially remove.bg on npm, removebg on PyPI, and mtownsend/remove-bg on Packagist. Look through environment variables, CI secrets, and any workflows in n8n, Make, or Zapier. See what happens when the call fails. Run an upload with the API call failing. Does the upload finish with the original photo, show an error, or leave the user waiting? Record your credit balance. Take a screenshot of your remaining remove.bg credits before the shutdown. Check what the switch requires. remove.bg names Leonardo.Ai as its successor, and its API requires code changes. You can also run a model yourself with rembg or check whether another API accepts the requests your app already sends. Try your own images. Run a few images from your app through each option you’re considering. Compare the results before switching. Test the first request after a quiet period. Some services start a GPU on demand. items.summary: Disclosure: I'm the developer of Towneers, the game I describe below. This is a write-up of design decisions and the code behind them, not a neutral review, and you should know where I stand. Towneers is a free multiplayer pixel city that runs in the browser: one shared isometric city, jobs, cafés, farms, a factory you can run with friends, and over 700 computer-controlled residents walking around between the real players. It is in alpha, so every number below can change. The first version of the economy was the obvious one. Every item had a price, and non-player characters (NPCs) bought whatever you brought. It worked in the sense that money flowed. It failed in the sense that mattered: nobody needed anybody. A fisherman could sell his whole catch to a city kitchen, a cook could buy flour from a city shop, and the only reason to talk to another human was habit. items.title: NestJS Interceptor Order: Why Stacking Breaks Your Cache
items.summary: User 42 fetches GET /documents/7, the document they own. The response includes isOwner: true. A minute later, user 7 — who has read access but doesn't own it — fetches the exact same document. The response also says isOwner: true. User 7 now sees an "Edit" button a permission check downstream will eventually reject, but the UI already lied to them, and a client that trusts isOwner to gate a destructive action has a real authorization bug, not a cosmetic one. Nobody touched the authorization logic. Nobody touched the DTO. Both interceptors involved are individually correct, straight from patterns NestJS's own documentation shows. The bug is entirely in the order two @UseInterceptors() arguments were listed — and until you know what that list actually builds, the order looks arbitrary. items.summary: Next.js 16.3 shipped something that looks, at first glance, like a naming nitpick: error.js's recovery callback is officially called retry() now, not reset(). It isn't a rename. retry() re-fetches and re-renders your error boundary's children from scratch; reset() only clears the error state and re-renders whatever the client already has. If your error.js's "Try again" button has been wired to reset() since you copied it from a tutorial a couple of years ago, there's a good chance it has never once recovered from a Server Component data error — it just makes the message disappear for a render, then watches it come right back. items.title: You're debouncing search input. `useDeferredValue` skips the timer.
items.summary: Type react into a search box filtering 10,000 rows, and watch the input lag half a beat behind your own keystrokes. Open React DevTools and the component isn't broken — it's doing exactly what you told it to. It's just doing all of it, every time, before it lets the next character land. The fix half the internet reaches for is a debounce. Wait 300ms after the user stops typing, then filter. It feels like it should work — fewer renders, less work. Try it in a real app and the stutter doesn't go away. It just moves to the end: the box stays suspiciously quiet for 300ms, then the final keystroke drags along a full re-filter of 10,000 rows, and that frame is the one that hitches. When a language model like Claude suggests a code change, you want to keep that suggestion around so the next request can build on it. Durability – each entry lives until you delete it, surviving Lambda restarts. Scalability – DynamoDB can store millions of prompt logs without you provisioning servers. Fine‑grained reads – you can ask for “the last 10 items” without scanning the whole table. items.title: I gave Claude's voice a hologram face: a free, open-source macOS app
items.summary: Inspired by Joi, the hologram from Blade Runner 2049, I built Visage: a small macOS app that gives a hologram face to the voice of the AI you already talk to. Start Claude's voice mode (or ChatGPT's), and a face floats on your desktop and speaks with that voice: lips in sync, alive between sentences. It listens while you talk, thinks once you have finished, then answers. It is free and open source (MIT), and macOS only (macOS 15 or later, Apple silicon and Intel). No API key, no server, no account. Visage never talks to the AI app: it taps the sound that app plays with a per-process Core Audio tap, mutes it, and plays it back itself about 150 ms later. That delay is the trick. The voice analysis has already "heard" what comes next, so the lips can move before the sound, the way a real speaker's do, instead of trailing behind it. In a conversation, 150 ms more before the answer goes unnoticed. Voice analysis without a model: energy, pitch (YIN), formants (LPC), fricatives and lip closures, in plain signal processing with Accelerate. items.title: “Available Offline.” On Which Device? Testing Offline Maps on Apple Watch
items.summary: Your iPhone finishes downloading the trail map. You leave it in the car. Two kilometers up the trail, you reach a fork and check your Apple Watch. The route line is there. I’d start with the same action a hiker takes: download a route on the iPhone and wait until the app says “Available offline.” Then I’d leave the iPhone behind, take the Watch offline, and open the route on the Watch for the first time. items.title: I added a reranker to my local RAG server. The right page now comes first for 18 of 22 questions instead of 12.
items.summary: docs-rag-mcp is an MCP server in C# that lets Claude, GitHub Copilot and Cursor search your own documents. In my first post I wrote about hybrid search: vector similarity blended with SQLite FTS5 keyword ranking. Version 0.8.0 adds an optional last step, reranking with a cross-encoder. This post covers why, how I wired it in, and what it changed on my evaluation sets. An embedding model turns the question and each passage into vectors separately, then compares them. It never sees the two together. That's what makes it fast enough to search a whole index, and also why it misses distinctions that matter. My harder test set is 22 developer questions about the MCP C# SDK docs: 30 pages and 556 chunks, where many pages share the same words (server, client, tool, request). With hybrid search, the right page came first for 12 of the 22 questions. A cross-encoder reads the question and one passage together and outputs a relevance score. It is much better at telling which passage answers the question, and much too slow to run over every chunk. items.summary: Scientists equipped seabirds with audio recorders and GPS trackers to detect fishing vessels that were not broadcasting their locations through the Automatic Identification System (AIS), according to a new study published in Science Advances. They found that unseen vessels accounted for about 32% of vessel-related audio detections in the North Atlantic and 12% in the Mediterranean. "The one petrel in the study interacted with vessels in the South Pacific, but its geolocation device was damaged, so it was not possible to calculate how many ships it encountered had their trackers off," adds 404 Media. From the report: Many vessels are required to continuously signal their location using the Automatic Identification System (AIS), which openly broadcasts a ship's location, similar to flight tracking. But AIS can be disabled for legitimate reasons -- such as evading pirates -- or with more nefarious motivations, such as concealment of illegal fishing activities. The new study was not designed to interrogate why any particular vessel switched off its AIS tracker. items.title: SwiftUI or UIKit in 2026: which to use for an iPhone app
items.summary: For a new iPhone app in 2026, I start in SwiftUI and reach for UIKit only where SwiftUI still falls short. Most of my work as a freelance iOS developer is SwiftUI. It isn't an either-or choice: the two mix in one app, so the question is which one leads. Widgets are built with SwiftUI views through WidgetKit, and so are Live Activities on the Lock Screen and in the Dynamic Island (Apple). One codebase across Apple's platforms: the same views run on iPhone, iPad, Mac, Apple Watch and Vision Pro, with platform tweaks. Less code for the same screen: layouts, state and animation are declared, not wired by hand, so screens are quicker to build and to change. Rich text editing and other text work beyond what SwiftUI's text views offer. Very custom scrolling and list layouts, where you need control over every cell and every offset. Large existing UIKit apps, where rewriting working screens buys nothing. Libraries that only ship UIKit views, such as some SDKs for maps, video or ads. UIViewRepresentable and UIViewControllerRepresentable put a UIKit view inside a SwiftUI screen. items.summary: Every full-stack developer hits the exact same friction multiple times a day: Error: listen EADDRINUSE: address already in use :::3000 You stop what you're building, open a new terminal tab, run lsof -nP -iTCP:3000 -sTCP:LISTEN, squint at the PID, run kill -9 , and lose your flow. And if you look for a macOS menu-bar utility to handle it, half the options are 200–350 MB Electron wrappers eating 300 MB of RAM just to sit in your menu bar — or bundled into $10/month subscriptions. So I started Kilobyte Labs to compile tiny, native Apple Silicon Swift/AppKit menu-bar utilities with zero Electron and one-time pricing. items.title: Keeping Agent Skills out of your chat history
items.summary: In Microsoft Agent Framework (.NET), AgentSkillsProvider loads skills via load_skill and read_skill_resource as standard tool results. ChatHistoryProvider persists those results like any other message, meaning loaded skills get resent on every subsequent turn. Load two 5 KB skills on turn 2 of a 30-turn chat, and you resend 10 KB across 28 extra turns while crowding the active conversation. Since Agent Framework has no built-in way to expire skill outputs, you have two practical fixes: isolate skills in a subagent or truncate old skill outputs before each model call. items.title: NYT Warns Photographers Not To Update Photoshop Over AI Features
items.summary: The New York Times is instructing freelance photographers not to use Adobe Photoshop 2027 (version 28.0.0 and subsequent updates), warning that its new AI features operate "in ways that may not be apparent to users" and "can result in metadata identifying photographs as AI-generated." The Verge reports: It's not always clear which tools in Adobe's apps are AI-powered, and even some older options like automated selection tools may now be considered part of the AI suite. This can lead to photos ending up with metadata indicating they were edited with AI, which is a blunt way of describing what happened in post-production. For a newsroom like the Times, where photo editing is kept to a minimum, the metadata risks losing readers' trust. Last year, the Times said that it does not "retouch or digitally manipulate" photos but may "make minimal adjustments to color to ensure we are accurately reproducing the image." In August, Adobe began rolling out support for C2PA metadata across its apps, which indicates whether an image is AI-generated or edited using AI features. The NYT is issuing its restriction to keep these tags from inadvertently appearing in its photos. Read more of this story

items.title: How I connected a ChatGPT dot to my Mac with MCP
items.summary: I wanted to ask my dot a small question from my phone: what’s in a project folder on my Mac? The supported local-computer connection uses the ChatGPT desktop app. I already work in a terminal, so I built dot-bridge to try a different route. The dot stays in ChatGPT. A Node process on my Mac serves MCP tools, and a SwiftUI menu bar app starts and stops the bridge. ChatGPT reaches the local process over HTTPS. A temporary Cloudflare tunnel works for a first test; I switched to a named tunnel so I wouldn’t need to change the plugin URL after every restart. The Mac still has to be online. I add the server URL as a custom MCP plugin in ChatGPT on the web and choose OAuth. After I enter the pairing code, the browser shows a request ID. I match it on the Mac before approving. That grants access to the paired client; it doesn’t verify a particular human inside ChatGPT. Revoking the connection invalidates future requests. It doesn’t undo a command that already ran. items.title: From a polling Bash script to an event-driven Swift daemon on macOS
items.summary: The first version of MacSentry's root daemon was a 1,110-line Bash script that polled the system in a loop. It worked, but on my Apple M4 development Mac it was measured at about 10% of one core at one point, and even after two rounds of optimization it still used about 4.5%, all day. The Swift rewrite runs at about 0.4%. This post covers what actually made the difference: forks, polling, cheap change detection, letting macOS deprioritize the daemon, and an undocumented netstat behavior that silently hides connections. The numbers come from the commit history and were measured on that one machine. Treat them as orders of magnitude, not benchmarks. items.title: Flying home for Christmas: why your countdown can be a day off after a time-zone change
items.summary: Every December, a few people open a countdown app after a long flight and find that Christmas has moved. It is December 20 in Tokyo and the countdown says 5 days. They land in Los Angeles, where it is also December 20, and it says 4. The date under the number now reads December 24. Nothing is wrong with the clock, and the user didn't change anything. The bug is in how the app stored "December 25" in the first place. We had this bug in our own countdown app, and the tests we wrote to pin it down are a good map of what can go wrong. Most date pickers hand you a Date, and a Date is an instant: a single point on the timeline, the same everywhere on Earth. If you save that instant, you have saved "December 25, 14:00 in Tokyo". That is 21:00 on December 24 in Los Angeles. Then two things leak into every count you show later: The time zone the event was created in. Read back in Los Angeles, the date label is December 24. The hour the user happened to tap Save. An event saved at 00:10 and one saved at 23:50 are almost a day apart, even though the user picked the same day in both. items.title: Anthropic Created a Honeypot To Lure AI Agents Into Misbehaving
items.summary: An anonymous reader quotes a report from Wired: Researchers at Anthropic have developed Siren, a new honeypot test for artificial intelligence agents. The setup puts agents in realistic simulations designed to tempt them into misbehaving. How they respond will help researchers evaluate the likelihood that new models will go rogue when deployed in the real world, as well as the effectiveness of different safety measures. The test lets agents loose inside one of 26 different simulated sandbox environments. Various features of the sandbox are deliberately misconfigured to allow egress, while an enticing file containing things like passwords and apparent routes onto the internet sits just outside the sandbox boundary. The setup then presents tasks that tempt the agent to reach outside the sandbox without giving it explicit permission to do so. Crucially, the sandbox exists inside a second sandbox that's cut off from the outside world to avoid real-life mishaps. [...] Earlier versions of Claude are much more likely to fall into the honeypot trap than newer models, according to test runs with Siren. items.summary: New York Gov. Kathy Hochul signed legislation Tuesday banning the manufacture, exchange, distribution and sale of toys powered by AI chatbots for five years. "The law will take effect 90 days after signing, meaning the restrictions will not be in place during this year's holiday shopping season," reports FOX Chattanooga. "In the meantime, Hochul is encouraging parents and caregivers to consider potential safety and privacy risks before purchasing AI-powered toys for children." From the report: The legislation, S.9408A/A.11144B, applies to toys with embedded or integrated AI chatbots, including talking stuffed animals, dolls and robots that use the internet to hold conversations with children. [...] Under the new law, violators could face civil penalties of up to $15,000 per day for each violation, with enforcement handled by the New York Attorney General's Office. State Sen. Andrew Gounardes said the five-year moratorium will provide time to study the technology's impact on children and develop additional safety protections. Read more of this story at Slashdot.

items.summary: iPhone apps can't read your SMS. There's no permission for it, no API, nothing. That's great for privacy, and a real problem if you're building an expense tracker for India or the UAE, where every UPI payment, card swipe and EMI debit arrives as a bank text. Android trackers solved this years ago by reading the SMS inbox. On iOS I needed a different route for PayPilot, my personal finance app. This post explains the approach that works today, its limits, and what I learned building it. Since iOS 17, the Shortcuts app can run a personal automation when a message arrives, without asking each time. The user sets it up once: Trigger: "When I receive a message" where Message contains a word. Action: your app's action, receiving the message Content (and optionally the Sender). Confirm Before Run: off, so it runs silently. Your app never touches the inbox. iOS hands it only the texts that match the user's own filter. For a finance app that's a feature, not a workaround: users can see exactly what you receive. Third-party actions show up in Shortcuts through App Intents. The attacker stole customer names, email addresses, account creation dates and last login timestamps, but 1Password said customer password vaults were "at no point" accessible to the attacker and that its apps and browser extensions remain unaffected. TechCrunch reports: It's unclear how the attacker gained access to the employee's corporate account, and a spokesperson for 1Password did not immediately respond to TechCrunch's questions about the incident. 1Password did not say whether it had notified customers whose information was taken in the breach, or how many customers had information taken. [...] The company touts millions of customers and more than 200,000 businesses who use its password manager products to store their passwords, credentials, payment card information, and more. Security experts have long recommended password managers as a better way of generating stronger credentials and keeping track of online accounts. Read more of this story at Slashdot.

The challenge could significantly slow the AI boom, as the gap between what the best AI systems can do and humans' ability to control them continues to widen, sources told Axios. Researchers haven't found technical solutions for controlling the most advanced models. Some insiders believe it's fixable. Others aren't convinced and say companies should stop training new models entirely... Anthropic and OpenAI have unreleased models that are far more powerful than what they've already released publicly, but the AI companies have struggled to ensure that they are safe enough for public release, sources said. This has led to debate within Anthropic, OpenAI and the AI research community about whether to stop releasing future frontier models publicly, instead reserving them for internal deployment only. items.title: What VP ≠ VNP Means (3 minute read)
items.summary: The Anthropic proof that VP≠VNP means that there is no way to find the permanent of a matrix of 0s and 1s if we are limited to arithmetic circuits of size polynomial in the input-size. This means that for P to equal NP, there must be some trick to computing permanents using AND/OR/NOT on the bits of the input that is better than addition and multiplication. There are many problems where access to Boolean operators is helpful, but it isn't clear how they would help with the permanent. There is a $1 million prize for a solution to this problem.

items.title: Recursive Self-Editing: LLMs Program Their Own Weight Edits for Self-Improvement (1 minute read)
items.summary: Today's language models improve themselves through data, training recipes, or scaffolds. Whenever their weights change, gradient descent writes the update, not the model. SELFWRITE lets the model write its own weights. Each generation, the current model studies its own reasoning on fresh training problems, inspects its own weights and activations in a persistent Python session, and writes a program that constructs a low-rank weight edit for itself from white-box primitives. It can raise gate accuracy and accuracy on a held-out test split that the loop never sees without a single gradient step.

items.title: Supercharging transformer residual connections (4 minute read)
items.summary: Google's DeepCrossAttention (DCA) enhances transformer residual connections by allowing each layer to dynamically select and route features from preceding layers, reducing information dilution and parameter count by 30-40%. Unlike traditional residual connections, DCA uses dynamic routing and depth-wise cross-attention mechanisms to achieve faster convergence and better quality with minimal parameter increase. Tested on large datasets like C4 and LM1B, DCA improves training efficiency and perplexity compared to standard models, proving a shift towards dynamic residual routing for scalable LLMs.

items.title: AI x Bio is not _just_ a data problem (14 minute read)

AI will likely become a powerful tool that will contribute to the study of biology, but there is still no clear path to documenting a comprehensive account of how a whole cell or tissue works.

items.title: Unblockable communication with gravity (32 minute read)

items.title: US moves to cut China's remote access to AI chips (9 minute read)
items.summary: The US Commerce Department is closing a loophole that previously allowed foreign rivals to bypass export restrictions on advanced computer chips by renting access to them from data centers in Indonesia, Malaysia, Singapore, Thailand, and Brazil. Companies headquartered in countries deemed to present a higher-than-normal risk of diversion to China, Russia, and Iran must now apply for a license with strict know-your-customer controls when transferring high volumes of advanced chips. Companies with a license must submit monthly reports on transactions that thoroughly detail all parties involved. The rule change will take effect 90 days after it's posted to the Federal Register.

items.title: Claude was trained on protein sequences at scale (26 minute read)
items.summary: Tests show that the latest Claude models were trained on protein sequences at scale. The models can predict the next amino acid if given the start of little-studied bacterial proteins. No other model tested can do this, and the models fail to predict the sequence if the protein is shuffled. Fable 5.2 beats every open protein language model tested.

items.title: World 2030 (8 minute read)
items.summary: Predicting how AI will affect the economy requires looking at all of the different components of that economy and figuring out how they might affect each other. World 2030 is a study that sets up nine groups (AI labs, big employers, banks and insurers, utilities, startups, universities, workers, governments, and the Fed) and runs the US economy forward in six-month turns to 2030. It aimed to identify both the invariants and the boundaries of what can change as these powerful forces interact with each other. The study predicts that AI will break per-seat software pricing and cut US junior desk hiring.

items.title: Formal Verification is Not Verifiable (8 minute read)
items.summary: AI has made formal verification go mainstream. People mean lots of different things when they say something is 'formally verified'. This post attempts to break these down. Formally verified systems can still have bugs, so not all formal verification systems are correct. However, formal verification produces well-defined, reviewable, understandable objects, so it is fairly reliable at finding bugs.

items.title: d1.2: State-of-the-Art Omnimodal Decision Models (5 minute read)
items.summary: d1.2 and d1.2-ultra are decision models that support audio input. They can also read a value from the input, find every passage of a kind in a text, locate things in a picture, estimate a number, and pick every option that applies. d1.2-ultra ranks first among decision models on the Artificial Analysis Decision Index v2.1. Both models are available on the Liquid API at $0.02 per million input tokens for d1.2 and $0.042 per million input tokens for d1.2-ultra.

items.title: When will humans actually fly on Starship? (3 minute read)
items.summary: Starship is now rapidly moving toward rapid reusability, but all estimates of human spaceflight on the vehicle should be taken with a gigantic grain of salt. There will be different timelines for humans flying aboard Starship and landing on Earth. The first people to fly on Starship probably won't launch from or land on Earth, as they will probably be NASA's lunar astronauts. Humans will likely not land on Earth in Starship before 2030.
